subject: gk
question: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
solution:
The correct answer is**__ __**__**Function of the President - France**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Function of President – France (Incorrect)
 
 
• India’s President is largely ceremonial (like UK), not executive.
 
• France has a semi-presidential system—its President holds real powers.
 
• Indian model is based on British parliamentary system, not French.
 
• Indian President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
 
• Thus, matching “Function of President – France” is not accurate.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rule of Law - Britain**

 
 
• Originated from A.V. Dicey, a British jurist.
 
• Emphasizes equality before law and supremacy of law.
 
• No one is above the law, including the government.
 
• Basis for Indian Constitution’s legal system and Article 14.
 
• Rule of Law is a foundational principle of British democracy
 
 
 
• **Procedure Established by Law - Japan**
 
 
• Japan follows the principle of "Procedure Established by Law" as mentioned in its Constitution.
 
• This principle implies that any law enacted by the legislature is valid if it follows the prescribed procedure, regardless of its fairness.
 
 
 
• Concurrent List – Australia 
 
 
• Borrowed from Australian Constitution.
 
• Both Union and States can legislate on subjects in this list.
 
• If there's a conflict, central law prevails (Article 254).
 
• India has 52 items (as of now) in the Concurrent List.
 
• Examples: education, forest, marriage, and adoption.
 
 
 
• **Separation of Powers**
 
 
• It is a doctrine that ensures the division of government responsibilities into distinct branches to prevent any one branch from exercising the core functions of another.
 
• The typical division includes the legislature, executive, and judiciary.
